# Kumārapetavatthu (Pv 41)

**Collection:** Sutta

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kumārapetavatthu* (Pv 41), translated as *The Prince*, is a verse narrative in the *Petavatthu* collection. The text illustrates the karmic retributions of indulging in excessive sensual pleasures and committing adultery, showing how such deeds lead to torment and rebirth as a ghost (*peta*) [Law 1926; Clark 1994].

Scholars of Buddhist monastic literature have noted thematic and textual connections between this story and other traditions. In his study and edition of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin *Abhisamācārikā Dharmāḥ*, Seishi Karashima observes verses in that Sanskrit Vinaya text that parallel or closely resemble verses found in the *Kumārapetavatthu* (specifically verse Pv 453, beginning *ayaṁ kumāro sīvathikāya chaḍḍito*) [Karashima 2012]. Modern comparative studies by Bimala Churn Law and Robert Warren Clark also cite the account of Kumārapeta as a prominent exemplar of the narrative motif wherein sexual misconduct results in severe post-mortem suffering [Law 1926; Clark 1994].

**Sources**

- [Karashima 2012] Seishi Karashima, Abhisamācārikā Dharmāḥ. Verhaltensregeln für buddhistische Mönche der Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādins (2012) — Identifies Sanskrit parallel verses in the Abhisamācārikā Dharmāḥ matching Kumārapetavatthu verse Pv 453.
- [Law 1926] Bimala Churn Law, Ancient Indian Tribes (1926) — Discusses the story of Kumarapeta in connection with adultery and karmic torments after death.
- [Clark 1994] Robert Warren Clark, Mara: Psychopathology and Evil in the Buddhism of India and Tibet (1994) — Discusses the motif of adultery leading to unfortunate rebirth in the Petavatthu account of Kumārapeta.
